problemText: Which of these is the best definition of tone in a piece of writing?
choices: The main character's personality and specific actions that move the story's plot forward
The personal emotional response that an individual reader experiences as they read the text
The attitude or feeling that a writer's specific words create toward the subject
The location and historical period in which the story's events are set and unfold
hints: Tone comes from the words on the page, not from the reader's own feelings.
Tone is about the attitude created by word choice, not about characters or setting.

problemText: Read this sentence: 'Marcus trudged up the stairs to his room after losing the game.' If you replaced 'trudged' with the neutral word 'walked,' what would change about the tone of the sentence?
choices: The sentence would gain more descriptive details and become more vivid through the use of a more commonly recognized action word
The sentence would communicate information more efficiently and become more appropriate for audiences who are still learning to read
The sentence would convey movement up a specific set of stairs more clearly and help readers better understand which staircase Marcus climbed
The sentence would sound less defeated and tired; 'walked' does not show effort or heaviness the way 'trudged' does
hints: Think about what feeling 'trudged' adds that 'walked' does not.
Use the swap test: say the sentence both ways and notice what disappears.

problemText: Which word in the following sentence carries the most feeling and does the most work to create the tone? 'The old woman whispered her secret to the young girl, glancing over her shoulder to make sure no one was listening.'
choices: whispered
old
secret
listening
hints: Look for the word that could be replaced with a plain synonym and would lose its special feeling.
The tone-carrying word is usually a verb or adjective that describes an action or feeling in a particular way.

problemText: Read these two versions of the same scene: VERSION A: 'The principal strutted into the auditorium, his shoes clicking loudly on the floor.' VERSION B: 'The principal walked into the auditorium, his shoes clicking loudly on the floor.' Which statement best explains what word choice difference creates in tone, and why?
choices: 'Walked' is preferable because it uses fewer letters and communicates the action more simply and straightforwardly to readers of all levels
'Strutted' makes the principal sound proud and confident, because when you swap it for 'walked,' the sense of deliberate, showy movement disappears
'Strutted' creates better sound effects in the sentence because it repeats the 'uh' sound found in other words and makes the passage more pleasant to read aloud
'Walked' accurately describes what the principal truly is, while 'strutted' misrepresents him as arrogant when he is actually a decent and honest person
hints: Name the specific word that carries the feeling, then say what feeling goes away when you swap it.
The answer should use the swap test and explain exactly what 'walked' would be missing compared to 'strutted'.

problemText: A student wrote this tone analysis: 'The sentence has a scary tone because the character is in danger.' Rewrite this analysis so that it correctly points to a specific word and explains what that word contributes. The sentence is: 'The stranger's eyes gleamed in the darkness as he moved closer.' Which revision best fixes the student's error?
choices: The word 'darkness' is most significant because in literature, dark settings have always been used to represent fear and frightening situations
The tone is scary because the sentence describes something scary and people naturally become nervous and anxious whenever they encounter scary ideas
The word 'gleamed' creates a sinister, threatening tone; if you swap it for the neutral word 'shone,' the eerie, predatory quality disappears
The word 'closer' makes the sentence scary because the stranger is physically approaching and drawing near, which is an inherently terrifying action in any story
hints: The correct answer names one specific word from the sentence and uses the swap test.
Avoid answers that describe a general feeling about the event or character instead of naming a word.

problemText: Read this paragraph: 'Maya devoured her lunch in the cafeteria while her friends nibbled their sandwiches. She barely paused between bites, while they picked at their food thoughtfully.' Using what you know about word choice and tone, explain which pair of contrasting words does the most work to show the difference in attitude between the characters. Then choose the answer that correctly names those words and proves their effect.
choices: 'Paused' and 'picked' are most important because they are both verbs that describe physical actions, and verbs always show a reader what characters are doing in a scene and how those actions might differ from one another

'Lunch' and 'sandwiches' reveal the contrast because they are nouns that name the specific foods being eaten, and the types of food people choose show important details about their habits and personal preferences in meals

'Cafeteria' is the strongest word choice because it names the specific location where the scene takes place, and knowing the exact setting helps readers understand why characters would behave and eat in particular ways around each other

'Devoured' and 'nibbled' show the difference because 'devoured' suggests eagerness and hunger while 'nibbled' suggests hesitation or lack of appetite; swapping both for 'ate' removes the contrast in energy and intention
hints: Find two words that are near-opposites in feeling and show what happens when you swap them both for a plain synonym.
The correct answer should explain what feeling each word carries and what disappears when you replace both with neutral words.

problemText: Which sentence contains a simile? Pay attention to the signal words like and as.
choices: The student's pencil was a sharpened point ready for the test.
Her voice rang out like a bell across the gymnasium.
The old clock ticked away the minutes before dismissal.
Time flew by during the field trip to the museum.
hints: Look for the word like or the word as in each choice.
A simile always signals a comparison with one of those two words.

problemText: Read the line from a story about a soccer game: 'The goalie's hands were iron, catching every shot that came her way.' What does this metaphor tell the reader about the goalie's hands?
choices: The goalie's hands were made of actual metal material that could conduct electricity.
The goalie's hands were cold and hard to the touch like frozen objects.
The goalie's hands were strong, hard, and reliable at stopping the ball.
The goalie's hands moved back and forth in the way that metal swings when pushed.
hints: Think about what iron is like: what quality does iron have that would describe a goalkeeper's skill?
The meaning is not about the material itself, but about the strength and dependability the comparison suggests.

problemText: A student reads this sentence: 'The ancient refrigerator hummed and rattled every time it cycled on.' Is this personification? Explain your choice.
choices: Yes, because the refrigerator makes sounds that indicate it has feelings and emotions like a person would.
No, because personification can only happen when comparing something to living things like plants or animals.
Yes, because hummed and rattled are both words that describe how people feel when they are nervous.
No, because hummed and rattled are literal sounds a refrigerator can actually make, not human qualities.
hints: Remember: personification requires a human quality like a feeling or a choice, not just any action or sound.
Ask yourself: can a refrigerator actually make those sounds on its own, or do they show a human emotion?

problemText: Read these two lines from a passage about a storm: (1) 'The wind howled like a pack of wolves attacking the house.' (2) 'The storm devoured the entire town with rain and thunder.' Identify the figurative device in each line, then explain what each one tells the reader about the intensity of the weather.
choices: Line 1 is a simile comparing the wind to wolves and suggesting violent, aggressive force; Line 2 is a metaphor suggesting the storm consumed or overwhelmed everything in its path.
Line 1 is a metaphor showing the wind is angry because it acts like a living thing; Line 2 is a simile showing the storm is destructive and harmful to buildings and people.
Line 1 is personification because wind cannot actually howl or attack like animals do; Line 2 is hyperbole because storms do not literally consume or eat towns the way living creatures do.

Line 1 uses the word 'like' to show two things are similar in how dangerous they are; Line 2 uses the word 'devoured' to show the storm is active and threatening, making the weather seem powerful and overwhelming.
hints: Line 1 contains a signal word that marks one device; Line 2 says the storm IS something without using like or as.
For Line 2, ask what 'devour' means and what it suggests about how completely the storm affected the town.

problemText: A student encounters this sentence: 'The leaves danced across the lawn in the autumn breeze.' The student says this is personification because leaves cannot dance. Is the student correct? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, the student is correct; leaves cannot literally dance, so any mention of dancing is personification.
Yes, the student is correct; danced gives the leaves a human action and movement, which is a human quality.
No, the student missed that this is a simile because the leaves are compared to dancers using the word like.
No, the student did not check whether danced is a sound; sounds are what mark personification.
hints: Personification is about giving human qualities to nonhuman things; dancing is something a person chooses to do.
Look at the definition: does the word danced describe a feeling or a choice that only something human can make?

problemText: Read this passage: 'I have asked my brother to do his chores a million times. Last week, I reminded him six times on Monday alone. His messy room is a disaster zone.' A classmate labels the first sentence as hyperbole and the third sentence as a metaphor, then adds no meanings. What would a complete answer include, and which label, if any, needs to be changed?
choices: Keep both labels; add that hyperbole shows the brother's refusal to help, and metaphor shows the room is very messy.
Keep the hyperbole label; change metaphor to personification; explain that the room is alive and causing trouble.
Keep both labels; add that hyperbole shows how many times the speaker asked, and metaphor shows the room is extremely untidy or chaotic.
Change hyperbole to personification; keep the metaphor label; explain that asking many times shows frustration, and the room being messy is bad.
hints: A complete answer always names the device AND states what it actually means in plain words, not just recognizing the label.
For the third sentence, check whether 'disaster zone' could be literally true: is a bedroom actually a zone of disasters?

problemText: Which of the following is a theme rather than a topic? Remember: a theme is a complete sentence that says something about people or life, while a topic is just a word or two naming what the story keeps circling.
choices: A general topic or subject word that names what a story explores without making a statement about life or people.
A single word or short phrase that identifies the main subject of a story but does not express a complete idea or claim.
A word that describes the main focus of a story but does not say anything meaningful about what the story teaches us about people or life.
Keeping a secret for too long can make it harder to share, even when you want to.
hints: A theme answers the question 'what does the story show about people?' not just 'what is this story about?'
Look for the choice that is a full sentence making a claim, not just a single word.

problemText: Read this story: 'Marco saved money for three months to buy a video game. The day he had enough, his best friend told him his own family could not afford to buy him anything for his birthday. Marco spent his game money on a gift for his friend instead. A week later, his friend gave Marco a handmade card that took him two days to make.' Which of the following is the topic of this story?
choices: Generosity
Generosity can feel better than getting what you planned to buy.
Friendship and sacrifice
Giving gifts is always the right choice.
hints: The topic names what the story circles around, in just one or two words.
The topic does not make a claim or tell a rule—it only names the subject.

problemText: A student wrote this summary of a story about a girl named Sofia who trained for a swimming competition: 'Sofia is an amazing athlete who trains for a race. She practices every day, which is pretty cool. In the race she swims really fast.' Which sentences in this summary contain opinions or judgments that should be removed?
choices: 'She practices every day' and 'In the race she swims really fast'
'Sofia is an amazing athlete' and 'which is pretty cool'
Only 'In the race she swims really fast'
Only 'She practices every day'
hints: Judgments are words that grade or rate something, like saying whether it is good, bad, or interesting.
Ask: would a reader who disliked this story disagree with those words?

problemText: Read this story: 'Jamal signed up to give a presentation in class but did not prepare. The night before, he asked his parents for help, and they showed him how to make a poster. The next morning he added a few of his own ideas. During the presentation, two kids asked him questions he could not answer, but when he admitted he did not know, they said they wanted to learn more anyway.' A student proposed this theme: 'You should always ask your parents for help when you are not ready.' Why is this not a good theme statement?
choices: The story does not mention school, so it cannot have a theme about school.
It is too short to be a real theme.
It starts with 'always,' which is a sign it is a rule or command, not a theme.
It only uses one detail from the story instead of two.
hints: Look at the key words at the start of the sentence. Words like 'always' and 'never' suggest you may have written a command instead of reporting what happened.
A good theme says what the story shows happening to people, not what people should do.

problemText: Read this story: 'Leo promised his younger cousin he would teach her to ride a bike over the summer. In July he was busy with camp, so he skipped two lessons. When he finally came back in August, his cousin would not ride with him because she felt he had forgotten about her. Leo apologized and wrote her a note explaining why he missed the lessons. The next day she agreed to practice with him, and they spent the last two weeks of summer riding every afternoon.' Which statement best describes the complete objective summary of this story?
choices: Leo taught his cousin to ride a bike over the summer because he made a promise, and by spending time with her in August and September they grew closer through their shared activity.

Leo missed some bike lessons in July because of camp and his cousin was hurt by this, but he wrote her a note apologizing and they eventually practiced riding together throughout the remainder of summer.
Leo promised his cousin he would teach her to ride a bike, went to camp in July, and came back in August to find that she was upset with him for missing lessons until he apologized to her.

Leo skips bike lessons in July because he is busy, but comes back in August. His cousin will not ride until he apologizes and explains why he missed the lessons. They then ride together for the rest of summer.
hints: An objective summary reports events in order and reaches the ending—it includes both the problem and how it turns out.
Cross out any choice that judges the story (calling something 'wonderful' or 'unfair') or leaves out a key event the ending depends on.

problemText: Read this story: 'Yuki painted a landscape for the school art show and hung it without a title. Three people asked her what it was supposed to be, and each time she said, "Whatever you see." A visitor spent ten minutes looking at it and then told her it reminded him of his childhood home, even though Yuki had painted a made-up place. Another visitor said it was the most confusing piece in the show and complained it had no name. Yuki's painting sold to the first visitor.' A student proposed this theme: 'A painting without a title is better than a painting with one.' To test whether a theme is strong, you should be able to find at least two separate details in the story that both support it. Using this test, explain why this theme would NOT be strong, even though the story does show a painting selling.
choices: The theme makes a comparison using 'better than,' but the story shows that people disagreed about its value, so it is not supported by two separate details that both point the same way.

One visitor complained the painting had no name and found it confusing, while another visitor loved the title-less painting so much he bought it, which means the story gives contradictory evidence rather than two details supporting the same point.

The story shows a visitor saying the untitled painting was confusing and another saying it reminded him of his home, but these details support opposite conclusions about whether having no title was good or bad.

The theme depends on proving that untitled paintings are better in general, but the story only shows one painting, and one visitor's opinion that it was confusing contradicts the idea that no title is an advantage.
hints: Apply the two-details test: say the theme sentence, then point to two different places in the text that both support it.
Look at what different people in the story believed about Yuki's painting. Did they all agree on whether no title was a good choice?

problemText: A story uses the pronouns he, she, and they throughout, and the narration goes inside the mind of exactly one character to show what that character thinks and feels. What is the point of view of this story?
choices: Third person limited
Third person omniscient
First person
Second person
hints: The question tells you the narration uses he, she, and they — not I or you.
Exactly one character's thoughts are shown, not two or more characters' thoughts.

problemText: Read this excerpt: "Maya pressed the doorbell and held her breath. She was sure Mrs. Chen would recognize the torn edge of the library book she was returning." Using the whose-thoughts test, determine what the narration allows the reader to know about this moment.
choices: The reader knows what both Maya and Mrs. Chen are thinking at the same time
The reader knows what Maya is thinking but not what Mrs. Chen is thinking
The reader knows only what Mrs. Chen is thinking, not what Maya thinks
The reader cannot know anyone's thoughts because the narration is told from outside the story
hints: Look at the sentence structure: which character's mind does the narration actually open up to the reader?
Remember that actions done by a character without the narration saying what they think or feel do not count as opening that character's thoughts.

problemText: A sentence in a story reads: "You duck under the low branch and feel the rough bark scrape your shoulder as you run toward the creek." This sentence is spoken by the narration, not by a character in dialogue. What point of view is being used?
choices: First person
Third person limited
Second person
Third person omniscient
hints: Pay attention to which pronoun the narration itself uses to speak to the reader.
The pronoun you in narration (not in quotation marks) is the signal for this point of view.

problemText: Read this passage: "Kenji looked out the window and wondered if his best friend was also staring at the rain, thinking about the cancelled game. Down the block, his best friend Akira sat on his porch and thought about the same thing — but about Kenji. They were thinking the same thoughts at the exact same moment, though neither one knew it." Explain why this passage cannot be first person or second person, and name the point of view that fits.
choices: This must be third person limited because it uses the names Kenji and Akira instead of pronouns like I or you throughout the narration
This must be first person because the narration reveals the private thoughts and feelings of one character wondering about what another character is thinking
This must be second person because the narration is written as a series of direct addresses to the reader about what both characters know and feel
This must be third person omniscient because the narration opens the thoughts of two different characters in the same passage
hints: Use the whose-thoughts test: count how many different characters' private thoughts or feelings the narration actually shows inside.
When the narration reveals something that two characters do not know about each other, it has gone inside both of their heads — that is the key mark of one particular point of view.

problemText: In a story, a character named Rosa says out loud to her friend, "I promise I saw a deer in the backyard this morning." The narration describing Rosa is in third person and goes: "Rosa promised she had seen a deer, though she was not entirely sure." Explain what makes the narration voice different from the character's voice, and identify what the reader can know that Rosa does not admit.
choices: The character Rosa speaks as I, but the narration speaks as she; the reader knows Rosa is uncertain even though she sounds certain out loud
The character Rosa speaks as I, but the narration speaks as she; the reader knows Rosa is deliberately choosing to lie to her friend about what she saw
The character Rosa speaks as I, but the narration speaks as she; the reader knows that Rosa's statement matches what actually happened in the backyard
The character Rosa speaks as I, but the narration speaks as she; the reader knows Rosa is hiding information that she will later share with someone else
hints: Look at what the narration privately reveals about Rosa's mind — what does it tell us that her spoken promise does not?
Remember that the narration's access to a character's thoughts can tell the reader something that character is hiding or not telling the truth about.

problemText: A story begins: "I have been the same red bicycle leaning against the garage wall for three years. In that time, I have never been ridden, and I have watched four different children walk past me on their way to the bus stop. I wonder if any of them ever notice the rust forming on my chain." Explain why the narrator cannot be the author of this story, and identify one thing you know about the narrator that is not a thought or a feeling but is still only knowable from the narration's point of view.
choices: The narrator is a bicycle because the text says 'red bicycle,' and an author is a person, so the author did not invent a person; something knowable only from the narrator's point of view is that the bicycle has been rusted

The narrator is a bicycle because it says I and refers to itself as a bicycle, and an author is a person; something knowable only from this narrator's view is that no one has ever ridden it for three years

The narrator is a bicycle because no real person could be a bicycle, so the author invented this voice as a made-up character; the narrator can see all the children walk by every day, something no bicycle in real life could do

The narrator must be a child because only a child could wonder about whether other children notice things, so the author pretended to be a child; something only the narrator could know is the feeling of being ignored
hints: Look for a detail in the narration that could never be true of the real, living author — that proves the narrator is invented.
After you prove the narrator is not the author, find something the narration reveals that goes beyond thoughts and feelings — something only someone in the bicycle's exact spot could observe or know.
